**Two Violins**

One gleamed a fiery red, hand-carved and freshly made—
Its maker, a local craftsman, had pried the seasoned wood
From the pew of a church long since unmade,
The Devil's instrument, wrenched from the house of God.
Yet it sang out merry and clear
Despite my faltering hand;
Bright and sharp as a young wine, they said,
Though in time it would soften and expand,
And I would grow to meet it.

The other wore a mellow yellow hue,
Its chin worn smooth with age,
Its varnish gleaming amber, Baltic-born and true,
Its back a single sheet of tiger maple's grain,
Its voice a low and shadowed timbre.
A century had passed, they said, since its birth—
Its sound, now fixed, would never change:
Rich and resonant upon the G and D,
Yet thin along the higher range.
How it had crossed from the Old World
Remained a matter of guess and lore—
Light as an exile's traveling case,
Its hollow body a vessel, and nothing more.

This was the one I chose,
Not the instrument of flame—
And teachers, pausing mid-lesson,
Would turn to trace the sorrow whence it came.

---

outputs.L3:
The shop smelled of rosin and old wood, and there, resting side by side on a strip of dark velvet, were the two violins I had come to choose between. The first was fire-red, its varnish so fresh it seemed to catch and hold the afternoon light like a coal pulled from the hearth. It had been hand-carved only months before, the scroll still crisp with the confidence of new work, every curve of the body announcing itself boldly. The second was yellow—not the bright, cheerful yellow of sunflowers, but something deeper, more amber, more aged. It was a full century old, and it wore its history quietly, without ostentation, the way an old man wears a coat that has long since molded itself to his shoulders.

The luthier, a wiry man with ink-stained fingers, told me the story of the red violin with evident relish. Its wood, he explained, had been salvaged from the pew of a church that was torn down some years back—oak that had once borne the weight of solemn worshippers, of bowed heads and folded hands, now reshaped into an instrument of decidedly different purpose. "The Devil's instrument," he said, laughing, "wrenched right out of God's house." He seemed delighted by the irony of it, this transformation of sacred wood into something that could summon such wild, dancing music. The violin practically hummed with mischief, as though it remembered its old pews and had decided, in its new incarnation, to have a bit of fun.

But it was the yellow violin that held my attention, that seemed to pull at something deeper than curiosity. Its varnish had been made with Baltic amber, the luthier explained, a technique passed down through generations of craftsmen who understood that some materials could not simply be manufactured—they had to be sourced, cured, coaxed into readiness across years. The back was cut from a single piece of tiger maple, its grain rippling like water frozen mid-current, each stripe of light and dark catching the eye differently depending on how you turned it. When he drew the bow across its strings to demonstrate, the sound that emerged was low and dark, almost mournful, a timbre that seemed to come from some place deeper than the wood itself. "This tone," he said, "will not change. Not in ten years, not in a hundred. It has already become what it will always be."

I chose the yellow violin. There was something about its age, its quiet insistence on the Old World from which it had come, that spoke to me more than the red violin's fiery charisma ever could. The red one seemed born entirely of the present—clever, ironic, a little proud of its own cleverness. The yellow one felt like it belonged to some other time altogether, carrying within its grain the specific weight of years I could never know, origins I could only guess at. There was a quality of emptiness in its sound, a kind of resonant hollow that seemed to invite rather than repel, as though the music it made was less something played than something recovered, drawn up from a well that had been sealed a long time ago.

I did not fully understand, in that moment, why the emptiness appealed to me more than the fire. But I understood it later, in lesson after lesson, when I would draw my bow across those amber-varnished strings and watch my teachers go still. They would be mid-sentence, mid-correction, and then the sound would come—that low, dark, aching note—and something in their faces would shift. They would turn, almost involuntarily, as though the sound itself had a gravity that pulled their attention physically toward its source. It was not virtuosity that caught them; I was, in those early years, far from skilled. It was something in the instrument itself, some inherited sorrow in its timbre that no amount of technique could fake and no amount of time could erase. I had chosen an instrument that already knew how to grieve, and it was teaching me, slowly, how to let it.
outputs.L4:
# Two Violins

The luthier held them both out to me like twin possibilities,
each one a different kind of promise.

The first was fire-red, freshly carved
from the salvaged wood of an old church pew—
you could almost smell the varnish still curing,
almost hear the hymns caught in its grain.
*This one will open up*, he said,
*give it ten years, twenty—
the sound will deepen, mellow,
find itself the way young wood always does.*
It gleamed like something not yet finished
becoming what it was.

The second was amber-yellow, a century worn
into its tiger-maple back, the stripes
of grain rippling like water under old varnish.
Its edges were nicked from hands
I would never know, its scroll
smoothed by a century of shoulders.
No one could say for certain where it came from—
some said Prague, some said a village
that didn't exist on maps anymore,
some said it had crossed an ocean
in the dark hold of a ship, wrapped in a coat
that belonged to someone's grandfather.

I lifted the bow to each in turn.

The red one sang bright and eager,
a voice still learning what it wanted to say.
The amber one exhaled something older—
a low, plaintive note that seemed to carry
the weight of every hand that had held it,
every room it had grieved in.
It did not shimmer. It ached.

I chose the second.

Not for its resale value, not for pedigree,
but because sorrow, when it is true,
does not need to be taught—
it has already lived.

Later, teachers would pause mid-lesson,
lower their own bows, and ask
*where did you find that sound?*
as if I had brought something back
from very far away,
as if the violin remembered
what I had not yet lived long enough to know,
and was, patiently, teaching it to me.
outputs.L5:
# The Weight of One Hand

There is something profound in the phrase "one hand"—two words that carry the weight of individual effort, of singular action against the vastness of the world.

Consider what one hand can do. It can write a letter, plant a seed, or reach out to steady someone who stumbles. History remembers moments when one hand tipped the scales—a signature on a document, a gesture that calmed a crowd, a touch that comforted the dying. We often imagine change requiring armies, movements, or grand coalitions, yet so much of what shapes our world begins with a single hand making a single choice.

The hand itself is a marvel of purpose and adaptability. It grips, releases, builds, and destroys. It can be closed into a fist or opened in offering. The same hand that strikes can also heal; the same hand that takes can also give. This duality makes the hand a fitting symbol for human agency itself—neither inherently good nor evil, but shaped entirely by the intention behind its movement.

And then there's "the"—perhaps the most overlooked word in language, yet essential for specificity. "The hand" is not just any hand; it is *the* hand that did something particular, that belongs to someone specific, that matters in this exact context. This small article transforms the abstract into the concrete, the general into the personal.

Together, these words remind us that significance often lives in the particular rather than the universal. It is not "hands" collectively that move history, but *one hand*—belonging to *the* person who decided to act when others hesitated. In a world that often celebrates scale and collective effort, there remains something quietly powerful about the solitary gesture, the individual choice, the one hand that reaches out and changes everything.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a narrative poem about choosing between two violins, one new and fiery, one old and worn, and what that choice says about identity.
counterfactuals.output:
# The Two Violins

The dealer set them side by side like twins
who'd grown up strangers—one all amber gloss,
its varnish catching light like something spun
from fire held just short of burning. New.
The scroll still sharp, the edges crisp, unworn,
a voice inside it waiting to be told
what kind of voice to be.

                                    The other lay
more quiet in its case, the wood gone dark
as steeped tea, grain worn smooth where thumbs
had pressed for something like two hundred years—
some players famous, others not, all gone,
their oils and doubts still living in the seams.
A crack once mended near the f-hole's curve
like a scar that had decided to be beautiful.

I picked the new one first. It answered fast,
bright and demanding, every note announcing
*here I am, hear how I burn.* It wanted
to be extraordinary now, this instant,
wanted no history but the one we'd make
together, starting clean. I felt young
holding it. Capable of anything
because nothing yet was true.

                                    Then the old one.
And the sound that came was not mine, not fully—
it was theirs too, the dead hands, the worn varnish,
a sorrow braided into every overtone
like the wood remembered being trees, remembered
weather, remembered all the songs it wasn't
enough to only play once and let go.
It didn't perform. It confessed.

                                    I stood there
in the dealer's narrow room, afternoon light
falling through dust the way it falls through years,
and understood the choice was never really
about the wood, the varnish, or the tone.

It was: do I want to be the fire
that hasn't found what it will burn for yet—
or do I want to be the thing that's burned,
and kept its shape, and softened into something
that carries every hand that shaped it, still
finds new music in the shapes of loss?

I bought the old one. Not because it's better—
some nights I think the new one would have taught me
things this one cannot, the boldness of beginning
without the weight of everyone before.

But I wanted to hold something that had lived,
to feel my own uncertain, fumbling hands
become one more chapter in a longer story,
to know that when I finally set it down
some other player's fingers, decades on,
will find the groove my playing wore into it,

and call it, simply, *home.*
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose a poem in the voice of a violinist recalling the two instruments they were offered as a child, describing their origins and sounds.
counterfactuals.output:
# Two Wooden Voices

The luthier's shop smelled of resin and rain
when I was seven, small hands, small frame,
and he laid before me two violins—
one born in a Saxon workshop, thin
spruce top pale as morning, ribs of maple
grown slow on some Bavarian hillside, staple
of factories that stamped out hundreds more,
each one a cousin, each one a chore
of craft repeated. Still, it sang—
bright, a little brash, its voice that rang
like a schoolyard bell, insistent, clean,
the kind of sound that cuts through, sharp and keen.

The second one was older, darker-grained,
its varnish deep as tea, a little stained
with what the old man called "the weather of Cremona"—
though he'd found it in a pawnshop, not the owner
of any pedigree he'd swear to. Still,
he said its belly came from some old mill
near where the Alps let go and become hills,
wood that had waited eighty years, all stilled
inside a tree before it ever rang.
Its voice was low, unhurried—didn't clang
or startle. It confided. Every note
seemed to rise up slowly from a throat
that had swallowed decades, held them, let them go
in tones the color of December snow—
soft-edged, a little sorrowful, but true,
the way an old man's laughter sometimes is, in view
of everything he's lost.

I chose the second.
Not because I understood—I reckoned
nothing then of provenance or price.
I chose it because it sounded like advice,
like something that had lived before it spoke.
The bright one I could still hear when I broke
into practice scales some mornings, missing
its easy shine, its unafraid, unlistening
brilliance. But the old wood taught me how
to listen back—to let an aged bough
still speak, still shiver when the bow comes near,
as if some tree remembers, through the years,
the shape of wind, and wants, before it's done,
to give that memory back to anyone
who'll hold it right, who'll draw the sound out slow,
who'll let the dark wood tell you what it knows.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a rhyming poem contrasting a brand-new violin made from a church pew with an antique violin from the "Old World," ending with the speaker's choice.
counterfactuals.output:
# Two Violins

In a shop where old wood learns to sing,
Two violins wait, each a different thing:
One carved fresh from a weathered church pew,
Its grain still whispering of sermons it knew,
The oak remembers a hundred years of prayer,
Of restless children and confessions laid bare.

The other came from across the sea,
An Old World master's craft, aged with history,
Spruce top gleaming beneath amber light,
Its scroll hand-carved on some Tyrolean night,
Three centuries of players have known its embrace,
Kings and gypsies alike found their place.

The church pew fiddle holds hymns in its bones,
Each knot in the wood like a memory of stones,
The luthier who built it heard something divine—
Not perfection of tone, but a truer design,
Rough-hewn from a bench where the faithful once kneeled,
Its imperfections becoming its shield.

The antique speaks with a practiced address,
Every curve honed to elegant excess,
Its voice is refined, aristocratic, and clear,
A pedigree proven through century and year,
Yet something feels distant, a polish too bright,
Like borrowed prestige dressed in inherited light.

I lift the pew-violin, feel its rough grain,
And something in me stirs, half joy, half pain—
This is no relic of privilege or throne,
But a chapel remembered, transformed into tone,
I choose the wood that has heard common prayer,
Over pedigreed strings from an aristocrat's air.

For music, I think, isn't born of the old,
Or measured in provenance, polish, or gold,
It's found in the splinters of what we once were,
The pews we sat in, worn smooth like fur—
I'll play what remembers the hymns that we sung,
Not the voice of a court, but the voice of the young.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Create a lyrical poem about instrument shopping—two violins, red and yellow—that uses sensory imagery of wood, varnish, and sound to explore memory and heritage.
counterfactuals.output:
# Two Violins

In the shop where dust motes drift like slow bows,
two violins hang from a velvet rack—
one the red of dried blood, of autumn's last leaf,
one the yellow of candlelight, of turning wheat.

The red one smells of cherry wood and old smoke,
its varnish deep as a wound that healed wrong,
grain lines like rivers on a grandmother's palm,
maps of a country I never learned to name.

The yellow one is lighter, honeyed maple,
amber going gold where the light finds it,
smooth as the inside of a wrist,
smelling faintly of resin and something like rain
on a roof I remember from childhood, or dreamed.

I lift the red one first. Its shoulder fits
against my collarbone like a question
asked in a language half-forgotten—
the bow draws out a note dark as tea,
bitter-sweet, an old woman humming
in a kitchen that no longer exists.

Then the yellow, and the sound is different:
brighter, thinner, like morning through curtains,
like a name called across a yard in summer.
I hear my mother's voice in it, somehow,
though she never played, never held wood to skin
and made it speak.

The shopkeeper watches, patient,
used to this—the way strangers become
suddenly ancestral, suddenly full
of grandfathers who fled with nothing
but a tune stuck in their throats,
of mothers who hummed while hanging laundry,
the pins in their mouths like small silver notes.

Wood remembers the tree it was,
the forest, the rain that swelled its rings.
Varnish remembers the hands that rubbed it in,
years of oil and patience and waiting.
And I, standing here between red and yellow,
between two songs I haven't learned yet—

I am trying to remember which color
my blood runs when I miss a place
I've never been, which note matches
the specific silence of a house
after everyone who spoke a certain language
has gone quiet for good.

I choose the red. Not for the sound—
though it is a sound like sorrow set to work—
but because when I close my eyes
and hold it to my throat,
I can almost hear the wood before it was wood,
almost hear the tree in the storm,
almost hear my grandmother
somewhere far off, singing.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

**The Selection**

She lifts the third one from its velvet cradle,
turns it like a question she's afraid to answer,
and the luthier says nothing, only watches
the way light pools along the tiger maple—
those flame-stripes rippling under amber varnish
like something frozen mid-escape, mid-burn.

He tells her: the top is spruce, close-grained,
cut slow from a tree that grew in shadow,
but the back—the back is pew wood,
salvaged from a chapel torn down in '54,
oak gone soft with a hundred years of kneeling,
of hands worn smooth on wood worn smoother still,
of hymns that soaked into the grain like rain.

*Everything that resonates has been through something,*
he says, and she almost laughs, almost doesn't.

The scroll curls like a question mark, unanswered.
The varnish—amber, russet, the color of held breath,
of tea gone cold, of light through a whiskey glass—
was brushed on thin, seven coats, seven waits,
each one drying in a dust-lit room
where nothing moved but time and settling grain.

She sets the bow against the string
and something old inside the wood wakes up—
not sound exactly, more the shadow sound throws,
a note that seems to grieve before it's finished singing,
as if the pew remembers every empty Sunday,
every couple married, buried, married again,
and the maple, tiger-striped, still holds
the shape of wind that bent it as a sapling,
years before it ever learned the word *farewell.*

She doesn't choose it. It chooses her instead—
the way old grief recognizes new,
the way a body finds the ache
it didn't know it carried
until the amber caught the light
and something underneath it
answered *yes.*
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
